SECTION: 2 Label Words are Anchors (Pages 2-5)

TOPICS: In-Context Learning (ICL), information flow, label words as anchors, attention mechanisms, model performance validation, experimental metrics, applications

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The hypothesis is that label words act as anchors in In-Context Learning (ICL), with H₁ stating label words gather information from demonstrations in shallow layers to form semantic representations for deeper layers, and H₂ stating the model extracts information from label words in deep layers to make predictions (Page 2)
- Experiments validate the hypothesis using GPT2-XL and GPT-J models, showing isolating label words in shallow layers impairs performance and attention to label words correlates with prediction probability (Page 2)
- An anchor re-weighting method boosts accuracy by 16.7% on average (Page 2)
- Input compression results in a 1.8x speedup in inference (Page 2)
- Error analysis links confusion to similar anchor representations (Page 2)
- A study on GPT2-XL uses three metrics—S_wp, S_pq, and S_ww—to analyze information flow from text parts to label words, from label words to prediction targets, and among all words respectively (Page 3)
- Results show S_wp is high in shallow layers and decreases, while S_pq is low in shallow layers and becomes dominant in deep layers (Page 3)
- S_pq and S_wp usually surpass S_ww, indicating label word interactions are more significant (Page 3)
- The proposed hypothesis is that label words function as anchors in ICL information flow (Page 3)
- Information flow is blocked by setting $A_{l}(p,i)$ to 0 where $p$ is a label word and $i < p$, affecting model behavior most when label words are isolated in the first 5 layers (Page 4)
- Isolating label words in the first 5 layers significantly impacts model predictions, while this effect diminishes in deeper layers (Page 4)
- Figure 4 shows isolation of label words in the first 5 layers has the most significant impact, while random non-label word isolation or isolation in last 5 layers has little effect (Page 4)
- AUCROC_l scores in deep layers approach 0.8, indicating strong correlation between attention on label words and model prediction (Page 5)
- Shallow layers contribute negligibly to cumulative contribution (R_l), with significant increases in middle and deep layers (Page 5)
- The paper introduces the term "Anchors" for label words, which play a crucial role in forming final predictions (Page 5)
- Applications based on the understanding include anchor re-weighting and context compression (Page 5)

The second stream investigates the inner working mechanism of ICL through different conceptual lenses, such as making an analogy of ICL to gradient descent (von Oswald et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2022) and viewing the process of ICL as a Bayesian inference (Xie et al., 2022). Our approach offers new insights and demonstrates the potential for leveraging this understanding to improve the effectiveness, efficiency, and interpretability of ICL. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we propose a hypothesis that label words serve as anchors in in-context learning for aggregating and distributing the task-relevant information flow. Experimental results with attention manipulation and analysis of predictions correlation consolidate the hypothesis holds well in GPT2-XL and GPT-J models. Inspired by the new understanding perspective, we propose three practical applications. First, an anchor re-weighting method is proposed to improve ICL accuracy. Second, we explore a demonstration compression technique to accelerate ICL inference. Lastly, we showcase an analysis framework to diagnose ICL errors on a real-world dataset. These promising applications again verify the hypothesis and open up new directions for future investigations on ICL. Limitations Our study, while providing valuable insights into in-context learning (ICL), has several limitations. Firstly, our research scope was limited to classification tasks and did not delve into the realm of generative tasks. Additionally, our hypothesis was only examined within conventional ICL paradigms, leaving other ICL paradigms such as the chain of thought prompting (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022) unexplored. Secondly, due to hardware constraints, we mainly investigated models up to a scale of 6 billion parameters. E Details for the Calculation of AUCROC Suppose the positions of the label words in the input  $x$  are  $p_1, \ldots, p_C$  (without loss of generality, we suppose  $p_i$  corresponds to the  $i$ th class), the targeted position is  $q$ , the sum of the attention ma trices of all attention heads at the  $l$  layer is  $A_{l}$ . We postulate that there's a strong correlation between the attention distributions on the label words of the target position  $(A_{l}(q,p_{1}),\dots,A_{l}(q,p_{C}))$  and the model's final prediction. We use the AUC-ROC score to quantify this correlation. We regard  $(A_{l}(q,p_{1}),\dots,A_{l}(q,p_{C}))$  as a classifier's prediction for the model output label (that is,  $A_{l}(q,p_{i})$  is equivalent to the probability of model outputting label  $i$ ), and compute the AUC-ROC value of this prediction relative to the actual model output. We denote this as  $\mathrm{AUCROC}_l$ . For the case with more demonstrations (Appendix F.1), we simply sum up all  $A_{l}(q,p)$  of the same class. We postulate that there's a strong correlation between the attention distributions on the label words of the target position  $(A_{l}(q,p_{1}),\dots,A_{l}(q,p_{C}))$  and the model's final prediction. We use the AUC-ROC score to quantify this correlation. We then compute the matrix  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}} = (\mathbf{q}_1 - \overline{\mathbf{q}},\dots,\mathbf{q}_T - \overline{\mathbf{q}})$  by subtracting the mean vector,  $\overline{\mathbf{q}}$  from each query vector. Subsequently, we determine the  $M$  directions,  $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_M$  , that correspond to the M largest variation directions for the centralized query vectors  $\hat{\mathbf{q}}_1,\dots,\hat{\mathbf{q}}_T$  . The  $i^{th}$  direction,  $\mathbf{v}_i$  , is chosen to maximize the variance of the projection of the centralized query vectors onto it, while also being orthogonal to the previously chosen directions,  $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_{i - 1}$  . This process can be formalized as follows: ··· We define  $\sigma_{i}$  as the square root of the variance of the projection of  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}$  onto the  $i^{th}$  direction, i.e.,  $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\left\{\mathbf{v}_i^\top\hat{\mathbf{Q}}\right\}}$ . To derive features  $\hat{\mathbf{k}}\mathrm{s}$ , we project the key vector  $\mathbf{k}$  onto the directions  $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_M$  and scale the projections by the corresponding standard deviations  $\sigma_{1},\ldots ,\sigma_{M}$ . Each feature,  $\hat{\mathbf{k}}_i$ , is thus calculated as  $\sigma_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{k}$ . We further examine the influence of  $M$  on the prediction confusion matrix, Confusion $i j^{\mathrm{pred}}$ , as depicted in Figure 14. Given the similarity in outcomes for various  $M$ , we settle on a value of  $M = 10$  for computation of Confusion $i j^{\mathrm{pred}}$ . K Calculation of Confusionij To gauge the true degree of confusion between categories  $i$  and  $k$  for a given model, we suggest utilizing the Confusion $_{ij}$  metric: First, we procure all test samples  $x_{t}$  bearing true labels  $i$  or  $k$ . We then obtain the probabilities  $p_{i}^{t}$  and  $p_{j}^{t}$  yielded by the model for categories  $i$  and  $k$ , respectively, on these samples. These probabilities are normalized to a total of 1. Essentially, we derive a classifier  $f$  that delivers the probabilities  $p_{i}^{t}$  and  $p_{j}^{t}$  for the categories  $i$  and  $k$  respectively, on the test samples  $x_{t}$ . By calculating the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) value of this classifier  $f$ , we get the degree of confusion between category  $i$  and  $k$ , termed as Confusion $_{ij}$ . The computed Confusionij is a value that never exceeds 1. The closer Confusionij approximates 1, the less pronounced the confusion, and vice versa. We use the above metric instead of directly analyzing the output labels of the model because previous work has indicated the issue of insufficient output probability calibration in ICL (Zhao et al., 2021), which is greatly affected by factors such as sample ordering and model preferences for specific label words. By leveraging our defined degree of confusion,  $\mathrm{Confusion}_{ij}$ , we can implicitly alleviate the disturbances arising from insufficient probability calibration on the output labels. This allows for a more accurate representation of the model's degree of confusion for different categories, mitigating the impact of randomness. We use the above metric instead of directly analyzing the output labels of the model because previous work has indicated the issue of insufficient output probability calibration in ICL (Zhao et al., 2021), which is greatly affected by factors such as sample ordering and model preferences for specific label words. By leveraging our defined degree of confusion,  $\mathrm{Confusion}_{ij}$ , we can implicitly alleviate the disturbances arising from insufficient probability calibration on the output labels. This allows for a more accurate representation of the model's degree of confusion for different categories, mitigating the impact of randomness.
L Reproducibility

In the supplementary material, we have provided codes that allow for the faithful replication of our experiments and subsequent result analysis. To ensure consistency and reproducibility across different devices, we have fixed the five random seeds to the values of 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46. We invite readers to delve into the code for additional implementation details that may arouse their interest.
